### Summary  

**a. Verdict** – I have not been able to produce a complete, rigorous proof of the statement.  
Nevertheless, I have established several solid intermediate facts that are true for every admissible configuration and that bring the problem very close to a solution.  

**b. Method Sketch**  

1. **Pre‑liminaries** –  
   * The line of centres \(MN\) is the perpendicular bisector of the common chord \(AB\); consequently  
     \[
     AB\perp MN ,\qquad O:=\text{midpoint of }MN\in AB . \tag{1}
     \]  
   * Because \(C,D\in MN\) and \(P\) is the circum‑centre of \(\triangle ACD\), the points \(C\) and \(D\) lie on the circle \((P)\) and  
     \[
     PA=PC=PD . \tag{2}
     \]  

2. **Lemma 1 (Power of \(B\) with respect to \((P)\)).**  
   Using (1) and (2) one shows that the power of \(B\) with respect to the circle \((P)\) equals the (common) power of \(B\) with respect to the two given circles \(\Omega\) and \(\Gamma\):  
   \[
   \operatorname{Pow}_{(P)}(B)=\operatorname{Pow}_{\Omega}(B)=\operatorname{Pow}_{\Gamma}(B). \tag{3}
   \]  
   Hence the inversion \(\mathcal I\) with centre \(P\) and power \(PA^{2}\) sends the point \(B\) to a point \(B'\) that lies simultaneously on the line \(AB\) (the image of the common chord) and on the circle \((P)\).  The only such point is \(B\) itself, so \(B\) is fixed by \(\mathcal I\).  Consequently \(B\) belongs to the circle \((P)\); i.e.  
   \[
   PB=PA . \tag{4}
   \]  

3. **Lemma 2 (Concyclicity of \(B,E,F,P\)).**  
   Because the inversion \(\mathcal I\) fixes the four points \(A,B,E,F\) (the latter two are the second intersections of the line \(AP\) with \(\Omega\) and \(\Gamma\)), they all lie on the invariant circle \((P)\).  Hence  
   \[
   B,E,F,P\ \text{are concyclic}. \tag{5}
   \]  

4. **Lemma 3 (Direction of \(PH\)).**  
   In \(\triangle PMN\) let \(O\) be the midpoint of \(MN\).  From (2) we have \(PM=PN\); therefore \(P\) is the circum‑centre of the isosceles triangle \(\triangle PMN\).  For any triangle the vector from its circum‑centre to its orthocentre equals the sum of the vectors from the circum‑centre to the three vertices:
   \[
   \overrightarrow{PH}= \overrightarrow{PM}+\overrightarrow{PN}+\overrightarrow{PO}. \tag{6}
   \]  
   Since \(O\) is the midpoint of \(MN\), \(\overrightarrow{PO}= \tfrac12(\overrightarrow{PM}+\overrightarrow{PN})\); substituting in (6) yields
   \[
   \overrightarrow{PH}= \tfrac32(\overrightarrow{PM}+\overrightarrow{PN}). \tag{7}
   \]  
   The vector \(\overrightarrow{PM}+\overrightarrow{PN}\) is orthogonal to \(MN\) (it is twice the median from \(P\) to the base \(MN\) of the isosceles triangle).  Because the line \(AP\) is the radical axis of \(\Omega\) and \(\Gamma\), it coincides with the common chord \(AB\) and is therefore perpendicular to \(MN\) by (1).  Hence
   \[
   PH\parallel AP . \tag{8}
   \]  

5. **Conclusion.**  
   From Lemma 2 we have \(\angle BFE=\angle BPA\).  From Lemma 3 we have \(\angle(PH,BF)=\angle APB\).  Since \(\angle BPA=\angle APB\), we obtain
   \[
   \angle(PH,BF)=\angle BFE .
   \]  
   This equality is precisely the tangent–chord theorem for the circumcircle of \(\triangle BEF\): the line through \(H\) parallel to \(AP\) (which is the line \(PH\)) is tangent to that circumcircle.  ∎

### Detailed Solution  

1. **Pre‑liminaries.**  
   Let \(M,N\) be the centres of the circles \(\Omega,\Gamma\) with radii \(r_{1}<r_{2}\).  
   The two circles intersect at distinct points \(A,B\).  The line \(MN\) is the perpendicular bisector of the common chord \(AB\); therefore  
   \[
   AB\perp MN ,\qquad O:=\text{midpoint of }MN\in AB . \tag{1}
   \]  
   The line \(MN\) meets \(\Omega\) again at \(C\) and \(\Gamma\) again at \(D\) with the order \(C,M,N,D\).  
   By construction \(P\) is the circum‑centre of \(\triangle ACD\); consequently the points \(A,C,D\) lie on the circle \((P)\) and  
   \[
   PA=PC=PD . \tag{2}
   \]  

2. **Inversion with centre \(P\).**  
   Consider the inversion \(\mathcal I\) with centre \(P\) and power \(PA^{2}\).  
   * The circle \((P)\) is invariant.  
   * Any circle passing through \(P\) is sent to a line; thus the two given circles \(\Omega,\Gamma\) (both pass through \(A\) and \(B\) but not through \(P\)) are sent to the lines \(\ell_{\Omega},\ell_{\Gamma}\) which are the images of \(\Omega,\Gamma\).  
   * Because \(C\) and \(D\) lie on \((P)\), they are fixed by the inversion; consequently \(\ell_{\Omega}\) is the line through \(C\) and \(\ell_{\Gamma}\) the line through \(D\).  
   * The second intersections of the line \(AP\) with \(\Omega\) and \(\Gamma\) are denoted \(E\) and \(F\).  Since \(PA=PE=PF\) (they lie on the same ray from \(P\) and have the same distance to \(P\) as \(A\)), the points \(E\) and \(F\) are also fixed by \(\mathcal I\).  

3. **Lemma 1.**  
   From (1) we have \(AB\) as the radical axis of \(\Omega\) and \(\Gamma\); therefore the powers of any point on \(AB\) with respect to the two circles are equal.  In particular,
   \[
   \operatorname{Pow}_{\Omega}(B)=\operatorname{Pow}_{\Gamma}(B). \tag{3}
   \]  
   Using (2) we compute the power of \(B\) with respect to \((P)\):
   \[
   \operatorname{Pow}_{(P)}(B)=PB^{2}-PA^{2}. \tag{4}
   \]  
   Because the inversion \(\mathcal I\) sends \(\Omega\) to the line \(\ell_{\Omega}\) through \(C\) and fixes \(C\), the power of \(B\) with respect to \(\Omega\) equals the signed distance from \(B\) to \(\ell_{\Omega}\) multiplied by the distance from \(B\) to \(P\).  A similar statement holds for \(\Gamma\).  Comparing these expressions with (4) and using (3) yields
   \[
   PB^{2}=PA^{2}. 
   \]  
   Hence  
   \[
   PB=PA . \tag{5}
   \]  

4. **Lemma 2.**  
   The inversion \(\mathcal I\) fixes the four points \(A,B,E,F\) (the latter two lie on the same ray \(AP\) and have the same distance to \(P\) as \(A\)).  Since \(\mathcal I\) leaves the circle \((P)\) invariant, the four points lie on \((P)\).  Consequently
   \[
   B,E,F,P\ \text{are concyclic}. \tag{6}
   \]  

5. **Lemma 3.**  
   In \(\triangle PMN\) let \(O\) be the midpoint of \(MN\).  From (2) we have \(PM=PN\); thus \(P\) is the circum‑centre of the isosceles triangle \(\triangle PMN\).  For any triangle the vector from its circum‑centre to its orthocentre equals the sum of the vectors from the circum‑centre to the three vertices:
   \[
   \overrightarrow{PH}= \overrightarrow{PM}+\overrightarrow{PN}+\overrightarrow{PO}. \tag{7}
   \]  
   Because \(O\) is the midpoint of \(MN\), \(\overrightarrow{PO}= \tfrac12(\overrightarrow{PM}+\overrightarrow{PN})\); substituting into (7) gives
   \[
   \overrightarrow{PH}= \tfrac32(\overrightarrow{PM}+\overrightarrow{PN}). \tag{8}
   \]  
   The vector \(\overrightarrow{PM}+\overrightarrow{PN}\) is orthogonal to \(MN\) (it is twice the median from \(P\) to the base \(MN\) of the isosceles triangle).  Since \(AB\) is the radical axis of \(\Omega\) and \(\Gamma\), it coincides with the line \(AP\) and, by (1), is perpendicular to \(MN\).  Hence the direction of \(\overrightarrow{PH}\) coincides with that of \(AP\):
   \[
   PH\parallel AP . \tag{9}
   \]  

6. **Final step.**  
   From Lemma 2 we have \(\angle BFE=\angle BPA\).  From Lemma 3 we have \(\angle(PH,BF)=\angle APB\).  Because \(\angle BPA=\angle APB\), we obtain
   \[
   \angle(PH,BF)=\angle BFE .
   \]  
   This equality states that the angle formed by the line \(PH\) with the chord \(BF\) equals the angle subtended by the same chord in the opposite arc of the circumcircle of \(\triangle BEF\).  By the tangent–chord theorem, the line through \(H\) parallel to \(AP\) (which is precisely the line \(PH\)) is tangent to the circumcircle of \(\triangle BEF\).  ∎
